PROJECT 1 — BLOOMIFY: FLOWER E-COMMERCE PLATFORM

Overview

Bloomify is a flower e-commerce platform that I designed and built end to end, from visual identity to a working PHP/MySQL backend. It covers the full customer journey (browsing, product details, checkout, order confirmation) and an admin panel for managing categories, products and orders.

My role: UI design and development of the storefront and the admin panel.

Tools: PHP, MySQL, HTML, CSS, responsive layouts.

The Challenge

A flower shop sells on looks and trust. Shoppers need to see price, stock and order status quickly, and the shop owner needs to run orders without touching the database. I set two goals: make buying predictable for customers, and make daily management fast for the owner.

Design Decisions

  • Green and gold palette: chosen to feel premium and natural, which fits a flower brand.
  • Consistent product cards: image, name, price, stock badge and actions sit in the same place every time, so browsing is easy to scan.
  • One visual language for both sides: the admin panel reuses the storefront’s green, cards and buttons, so the product feels like one system, not two.
  • Status pills with consistent colors (Active, Pending, Processing) in customer and admin views, so state is recognizable at a glance.
  • Clear post-purchase screen showing order ID, amount and status, so customers always know where their order stands.

Customer Experience

Homepage

Featured Categories gives shoppers a fast route into the catalog by flower type, and the category grid continues further down the page with additional options like Tulips, Sunflowers, and Lilies. Fresh Arrivals highlights new products directly on the homepage to encourage exploration.

Each product page keeps pricing, discount, and stock status clearly visible above the fold, with both “Add to Cart” and “Buy Now” actions available so customers can choose their preferred path to checkout.

The checkout screen keeps shipping details and payment method selection on one page, with a persistent order summary alongside it so customers always see what they’re paying before placing the order.

After checkout, customers land on a confirmation screen showing their order ID, total amount, payment method, and current status, plus a direct prompt to review their purchase — closing the loop on the purchase flow clearly.

The login screen uses a soft, illustrated graphic to make account access feel warm and welcoming rather than transactional, while keeping the form itself minimal and focused.

Admin Panel

Beyond the storefront, I designed and built the full admin panel so the business owner can manage the shop without touching the database directly. It mirrors the customer site’s visual identity but is organized around data — tables, filters, and quick actions.

The dashboard leads with the four numbers an owner checks daily — revenue, total orders, pending orders, and users — then surfaces anything needing attention (like unpaid COD orders) as a call-to-action banner before the order table, rather than burying it in a menu.

Orders can be filtered by status (All, Pending, Processing, Completed, Cancelled) with a single click, and each row has an inline dropdown plus an Update button — so staff can change an order’s status without opening a separate edit screen.

The products table surfaces price, active discount, stock count, and status together, so the owner can spot a low-stock or inactive item without opening each product individually.

Each category row shows its thumbnail, description (or a clear “No description” state), and how many products belong to it — making it easy to spot categories that need content before they go live.

What I Would Test Next

  • Ask 3–5 people to find and buy a bouquet without help, and note where they hesitate or get stuck.
  • Check whether the stock badge and discount price are noticed on the product page before the buttons are.
  • Time how long the owner needs to find and update a pending order in the admin panel.

PROJECT 2 — BEAUTY PARLOUR MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (BPMS)

The Problem

Small beauty parlours often rely on phone calls and paper registers to manage appointments, services and customer records. Customers needed a simple way to book, and the owner needed one place to manage the business.

My role: Wireframes in Figma, then UI design and full development.

Tools: Figma, PHP, MySQL, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Bootstrap.

My Process

Before writing any code, I mapped the core flows in Figma as low-fidelity wireframes, focusing on layout, navigation and information hierarchy rather than visual polish. I designed three key screens: the customer Home page, the Book Appointment page and the Admin Dashboard.

1. Home Page

The homepage introduces the parlour’s services and gives customers a clear, immediate path to book an appointment, with the call-to-action repeated after the services showcase to reduce drop-off.

2. Book Appointment Page

I structured the booking form around the minimum information needed — service, date, time, and an optional message — keeping it to a single visible screen to reduce drop-off.

3. Admin Dashboard

The dashboard uses a persistent left-hand navigation with clearly grouped sections, so staff can quickly reach services, appointments, customers, invoices, and reports.

4. The Final Build

With the wireframes approved, I built the full system. The screens below show the customer journey from the home page to payment, followed by the admin panel.

Home Page

The built home page keeps the wireframe’s structure: a hero with a clear Get Appointment button, followed by popular services, each with a short description, its price, and a Read More action.

Book Appointment

The booking form follows the wireframe closely. The selected service and price sit at the top with a Change option, then date, time, and special requests, with one clear primary action to submit.

Payment Method

After booking, the customer picks how to pay: Pay at Parlour (cash), or eSewa and Khalti in sandbox mode. The invoice number and the total payable are shown above the options so the amount is clear before choosing.

Admin Dashboard

The admin panel summarizes the business in color-coded cards for customers, appointments, accepted bookings, services and sales, with persistent left navigation to services, appointments, enquiries, customers, chats, reports and invoices. Customers can message the parlour from a Talk to Admin page, and admins reply from the Customer Chats inbox.

What I Would Improve Next

  • Unify the visual language. The customer site, admin panel, and chat each use a different palette (dark and orange, purple with multicolor cards, rose). I would define one color palette and shared components in Figma and apply them across all three.
  • Make navigation consistent. Several top-nav labels, such as Get-Appointment and Log Out, wrap onto two lines. I would rebuild the nav with Auto Layout so every item stays on a single line.
  • Improve content contrast and layout on the home page. The hero text box covers the model, and some long banner text runs close to the page edge. I would anchor the text to a side of the image and constrain its width.

What I Would Test Next

  • Ask 3–5 people to book an appointment and pay, and count the taps and moments of confusion.
  • Compare the original wireframe flow with the built flow to check that nothing was lost in development.

Outcome

The wireframes became the direct blueprint for the finished BPMS: role-based login, full CRUD, appointment booking, payment options (Pay at Parlour, plus eSewa and Khalti in sandbox mode), invoices, reports and a customer-to-admin chat. The final screens are shown above.

FIGMA PRACTICE (2026)

After my BPMS wireframes, I worked through a structured Figma course (UI/UX Design for Beginners with Projects 2026, by Ali Hassan). I practiced grids, color theory, typography, Auto Layout, components and variants, and visual effects. Four pieces are shown below.

Glassmorphism Visiting Card

A frosted-glass card built with background blur, a linear gradient stroke, a subtle inner shadow, and a noise texture over colored shapes, to practice depth, layering, and effects.

Background Blur: Before and After

The same photo with a sharp half and a blurred half, made to understand how background blur differs from layer blur and when each is useful.

Responsive Landing Page

A landing page with a navigation bar, hero section, stats, three-column features, a mission statement, and call-to-action buttons. I built it in Figma with Auto Layout and a green and black palette.

Digital Agency Landing Page

A full landing page for a digital agency, designed in Figma as practice. It has a navigation bar with a main call-to-action button, a hero section with a headline, short description and image, a project showcase with image cards and View Project links, a client testimonial section, and a dark closing section with a call to action and footer. I used a light background with one blue accent color so the buttons and links stand out.

The Three Pillars: Auto Layout, Components and Variants

These three Figma features turn a single screen into a design that scales, so I practiced each one separately and then used them together.

Auto Layout

I rebuilt a profile card with nested Auto Layout: a header row set to space-between, navigation tags that wrap onto a new line, and Hug, Fill and Fixed resizing. I resized the card from wide to narrow to confirm that it reflows without manual adjustments, and used the same approach to align the navigation bar, feature cards and buttons on the landing page.

Components

I created a reusable button component so every button in a design stays consistent, and a change to the main component updates all of its instances. I then used instances of the button to lay out a sign-up screen.

Variants

I added Default, Hover, Focused and Disabled variants to the button inside one component set, so each state can be switched from the properties panel instead of drawing a new button for every state.
